🟢 Intro
- Most investors lose money in crypto, not necessarily because they pick the wrong assets, but because they fall into predictable, recurring traps. This week, Cyrus breaks down the 10 biggest traps every investor must avoid to survive and truly make it in this space.

🟢 Self-custody: a trap?
- "Not your keys, not your coins" is, for Cyrus, one of the most unfortunate quotes in crypto. Roughly 20% of all bitcoins have been permanently lost.
- Cold wallets and hardware wallets, long presented as the ultimate solution, have been hacked several times. Self-custody can be excellent, but only if you're extremely responsible and well organized (passing on your keys when you die, complicated trusts to manage, etc.).
- For most people, the best option isn't self-custody, but a regulated, trusted party (exchange, bank) that puts smart safeguards in place: MPC, asset segregation, and withdrawal protection like SwissBorg does.
- Ledger and Trezor seem better than some competitors, but 100% safe? That's not for him to say.

🟢 Good project ≠ good investment
- Everyone falls for it: "great tech, good project, so I'll invest." But does the token actually capture that value?
- Tokenomics is what you should look at first. Kamino and Morpho are doing tremendous work, but their token doesn't yet have clear buybacks or well-implemented governance. Hyperliquid (HYPE), on the other hand, combines great tech, a great product AND solid tokenomics.
- A project can turn things around: Morpho, for example, is putting smart mechanisms in place to bring more buy pressure.
- The real question: are you actually using the token? Proof-of-stake L1s have a strong thesis (you buy, you stake, you earn a yield from validated transactions), but many L1s have great tech with no real transactions behind it.

🟢 Token unlocks
- Back in the day, with ICOs (like SwissBorg's), you could sell your tokens right at day-one listing. Policies have changed since.
- An unlock means vested tokens that gradually get released. Many projects have a great token but huge unlocks coming.
- These unlocks often come from VCs. They're not all vultures, but they have a clear mandate: outperform the market (often Bitcoin). So they take profits when tokens are liquid in order to pay dividends back to their LPs.
- Watch closely: how and when the unlocks will happen, what percentage hits the market, and whether there's a sufficient buyback mechanism.

🟢 Yields too good to be true
- High yields on Bitcoin, Solana, Ethereum, stablecoins... remember Terra.
- A very high yield on an asset means either strong inflation of that asset (staking a token and getting back 20-30% means 20-30% is being reinjected into the market), or an over-leveraged, very risky bet (as with stablecoins).
- The golden rule: if you don't know where the yield comes from, then you are the yield. You're taking part in a potentially Ponzi-like scheme.
- On already very risky assets (BTC, ETH, SOL), don't expect a nice yield. The yield is the asset itself: keep it as is, or do liquid staking that actually makes sense.

🟢 Core vs satellite
- The biggest mistake: not distinguishing the assets you hold long term (core) from the ones you trade within the cycle (satellites, 2-3 years max).
- You never start a position directly in your core. You start with satellites, and after a cycle, you keep the ones that have proven themselves.
- You need to test a project for at least one cycle before moving it into your core. In crypto, most projects don't survive more than one or two cycles, often just one.
- The winning move: sell a big chunk of the satellite during the cycle, then buy back 50-90% cheaper in the next cycle if you still believe in it, to build it into your core.
- Cyrus's examples: HYPE seen at 40-70, bought back between 20 and 40; Solana seen up to 150, bought back between 20 and 30, then again at 70.

🟢 Selling at a loss
- Cyrus's personal example: 80k of Arbitrum ending up at 5k, losing trades you don't cut hoping they'll bounce back. Wrong mindset.
- You have to know how to cut positions and realize your losses. In crypto, if you don't cut, losses often go to zero (unlike stocks).
- The opportunity cost is huge: that Arbitrum could have been in Solana, in HYPE, or on a new bet.
- Sandbox example: from 30k down to 1-3k. Better to put those 3k into something you strongly believe in that could do a 4-5x.
- Even in stocks: Alibaba sold around 170-180, ten years later it's at 120. Even an excellent company doesn't necessarily bounce back. Keep only your winning positions, cut the losers.

🟢 Crypto influencers
- Cyrus doesn't consider himself an influencer, but an entrepreneur. Above all, listen to yourself.
- Some creators are worth respecting (he mentions Ivan on Tech and Virtual Bacon) for their holistic view and trading skills.
- Others just use you to sell and pump their bags, then exit. When an influencer sets a "target price," he often sells right after.
- The mechanism: he announces a 150k target while his real target is 100k. People buy at 99-100k, and he exits his position while everyone else buys the 100-to-150k trade.
- These influencers have multiple wallets, very hard to track, and work with centralized market makers who offload liquidity for their clients (see ZachXBT's accusations). This has been the case for the biggest projects.

🟢 "This time it's different"
- Every cycle, when everything's going well, we tell ourselves "this time it's different."
- Cyrus always works with 3 scenarios: bearish, base case, bullish. The last cycle stayed in the base case without hitting the bearish one (BTC: bearish 100k, base 125k, bull 200k, played out fairly well; Ethereum completely missed, Solana above expectations).
- Advice: set a base case where you could exit, and if you hit the bearish case, start auto-investing out across several tokens.
- Example: if you hit 100k, it doesn't matter, it's the bearish case, you can start exiting over 3 months, or set trigger orders (sell at +10%, +20%, at 120k...).
- Reminder: every cycle brings the same emotions. Right now we're at the lows (volume, content, everything), the calm just before the next pump (NFA).

🟢 Waiting for the perfect entry
- Everyone wants the best moment to get in. But that moment never comes.
- The football match analogy: the match lasts 90 minutes, but trying to watch only the goal moments doesn't work. You have to watch the whole match.
- You can play with trigger orders and trade the market (useful if you're good at it), but for your core portfolio, auto-invest remains the best approach.
- You can tweak your auto-invest: e.g. €10,000 over 3-4 years, so ~200/month. If the market looks like it's at a good level (low prices), you can load up more at the start (250, 300 instead of 200).
- Don't try to time the market. Aim to spend the most time in the market to catch all the goals scored during the match.

🟢 Trading solo
- Something nobody talks about: trading and investing on your own is very hard.
- The rat drug experiment analogy: an isolated rat facing drugged water always ends up dying, but in a "rat city" (a rich social environment), none of them die. They sometimes use, but they get through it.
- Trading isn't a drug, it's a means to reach financial freedom. But you go through extreme emotions, sometimes very painful, sometimes very satisfying.
- SwissBorg's strength is the community: helping each other, learning from one another, understanding where the light at the end of the tunnel is, and getting through it together.
- The Cyborg Advisor (in the works for months, coming soon), the Guardians, this show, and real-life meetups are all ways to share ideas and invest better, together.

4 stages of LLM training, clearly explained:

(a popular LLM interview question; bookmark this)

→ Pre-training
→ Instruction fine-tuning
→ Preference fine-tuning
→ Reasoning fine-tuning

The visual covers all of them.

A base model treats a question as text to be continued, not a request to be answered. Questions in its training data usually have more questions next to them, so that's what the model replies.

The stages after pre-training allow changing that behaviour, and each one uses a different training signal to do it.

0) Randomly initialized model

The weights are random numbers, so token selection is close to uniform, and the LLM outputs gibberish text.

1) Pre-training

The model reads a large text corpus and repeatedly predicts the next word.

This stage teaches the model grammar and facts about the world.

Also, most of its raw reasoning ability comes from this stage, and it's where nearly all of the training compute goes.

The model becomes good at continuing text, but nothing in the objective connects a question to an answer.

2) Instruction fine-tuning

Here, it trains on pairs of instructions and good responses, so it picks up the convention that a question should get an answer and a request to summarise should get a summary.

OpenAI used roughly 13,000 human-written examples on GPT-3, against a pre-training corpus of hundreds of billions of words.

The knowledge was already in the weights, and this stage mostly taught a response format.

3) Preference fine-tuning

A lot of requests have no single correct answer, and supervised fine-tuning needs a specific target to train against.

In this setup, two responses go to a human who picks the better one. You may have already seen this in ChatGPT, where it asks which of the two responses is better.

Those picks train a separate model that predicts which response a human would have chosen. The main model then gets updated to score higher against that predictor.

4) Reasoning fine-tuning

For maths and code, there's usually one correct answer, and a program can check it. Human preference isn't needed here, since correctness is already a usable reward signal.

The model attempts a problem, the answer gets checked, and it's rewarded when it gets it right.

DeepSeek trained R1 this way with GRPO, and behaviours like working through intermediate steps and going back to fix its own mistakes showed up during training without any examples demonstrating them.

That said, stage 4 only works when a program can check the answer. Maths and code inherently provide that.

But a support reply, a RAG answer, or a summary has no correct output to check against, so the reward has to come from somewhere else.

I wrote a full breakdown of how labs are handling that problem, from RLHF through GRPO, and what replaced the checker.

It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture!

If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have.

We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.

To get there, we need three things in my opinion:

- Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks
- Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them
- Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders

If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger. 

And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more.

It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!
